items.title: Adidas Officially Launches Limited-Edition Pokémon Collection
items.content_text: Adidas just dropped its limited-edition Pokémon collection , the latest in a pretty wild list of collaborations celebrating the franchise’s 30th anniversary. The full collection includes over 10 new designs for a mix of the company’s most popular sneaker styles, including the Samba and Superstar II. Each shoe has an entirely distinct look inspired by a specific Pokémon, and the stars of the show aren’t too surprising. Prices range from $60 to $180 with full family sizing. Even better? Every sneaker is available to buy right now. Adidas Just Dropped Its 30th Anniversary Pokémon Collection See the collection at Sole Play See the collection at Adidas See the collection at Foot Locker Some features, like the gold embroidered Pokémon x Adidas logo, appear across the collection, but each shoe generally stands on its own two feet (get it) as a unique release. Here’s the full list of what’s available in specific styles: Every New Sneaker in the Adidas x Pokémon Collection Pikachu - Superstar II (Yellow) and Superstar II (White) Gastly - Adistar Control 3 (Out of Stock) Haunter - Adistar Control 5 Gengar - Adistar XLG 2.0 (Out of Stock) Charmander - Superstar II Charmeleon - Superstar II Charizard - Superstar Vintage Rayquaza - Adistar Control 5 Mewtwo - Samba As you can tell, the collection includes a mix of full evolution lines (i.e. Charmander to Charizard) as well as some particularly iconic individual Pokémon like Pikachu and Mewtwo. I got the chance to check out three specific shoes from the collection of time, and let’s just say I’m impressed. I don’t typically go for the most colorful looks in the world, but the designs have a range of boldness that lets you pick a vibe that goes best with your style. And, of course, based on whichever Pokémon you like best. The Mewtwo Superstars are a soft purple with a sleek iridescent sheen. While every shoe includes a token-esque shoelace charm with its featured Pokémon’s face, this pair also comes with a funky “liquid” tag featuring the legendary’s classic Psystrike move. On the bolder side, the Charmander sneakers show a full graphic of the Pokémon blowing some literal Ember into the iconic Samba stripes. It’s cool to see each shoe get its own little deep cut reference to a Pokémon’s type and even specific moveset. The (new!) illustrations of each Pokemon are all high quality, and the shoes themselves are, as you’d expect, pretty darn comfy. As a limited-edition collection, it’s worth noting that stock may be limited. The Pokémon TCG side of things has been plagued by an ongoing scalping crisis that, these days, seems to extend to anything connected to the Nintendo franchise. Speaking of, the collection forms part of some pretty extensive celebrations for Pokémon’s 30th anniversary. The beloved media powerhouse currently stands as the highest-grossing franchise of all time, and has already launched unique anniversary collaborations with Puma , Crocs , and even Krispy Kreme . I’m sure we’ll see plenty of more announcements through the end of the year, which, at the very least, will bring us slightly closer to the next mainline Pokemon generation .
items.title_en: Adidas Officially Launches Limited-Edition Pokémon Collection

items.title: Microsoft Signals Intention to Close Down Ninja Theory After Deals to Save the Hellblade Developer Fall Through
items.excerpt: Microsoft has signalled its intention to close down Hellblade developer Ninja Theory after two deals to save the Xbox studio fell through.
items.content_text: Microsoft has signalled its intention to close down Hellblade developer Ninja Theory after two deals to save the Xbox studio fell through. In-line with UK employment law, a consultation with the staff at the Cambridge-based studio has begun. While Microsoft has said it is now working to close the studio, it remains open to an agreement to rescue the company. "Unfortunately, two separate agreements for Ninja Theory fell through," Xbox Chief Content Officer Matt Booty said in a blog post issued today. "We will now begin consultation with employees on a proposed closure while continuing to explore other paths forward." In June, at an Xbox Games Showcase event, Microsoft announced Senua, the third game in the Hellblade series. At the time, there was little concern about the game’s release. Indeed, there was little concern, publicly at least, about Ninja Theory itself. But that all changed when optimism sparked by the positive showcase was shattered by new Xbox CEO Asha Sharma’s “reset” memo, which suggested mass layoffs and studio closures were to come. Confirmation came in July, when Ninja Theory was among the studios on the Xbox chopping block. Amid the reports, fans expressed confusion at how Microsoft could announce Senua from Ninja Theory and then just days later tell the studio’s staff it planned to shut the company down. According to Game File , Microsoft allegedly planned to close or spin off Ninja Theory when it revealed Senua, and it did so thinking that “the promise of a newly announced game would help draw investor interest in the studio.” Clearly, that plan has failed. Will Senua ever come out? IGN has yet to comment, but it’s looking increasingly unlikely unless a dramatic, 11th-hour deal can be struck that would save not just the studio, but the Hellblade franchise. Perhaps giving Ninja Theory hope is that Psychonauts developer Double Fine and South of Midnight developer Compulsion both navigated their way to independence and brought their intellectual property along with them, as well as funding for new games. Microsoft, it seems, is willing to part with IP to help get its studios out the door. Ninja Theory’s Hellblade games have struggled commercially, and Microsoft is currently doubling down on its big franchises in a bid to raise revenue and profitability. It’s focusing on the likes of Minecraft, Halo (which is now under Activision’s umbrella), Fallout, and The Elder Scrolls as it looks to turn around the Xbox business over the next few years. For more on all the big changes at Xbox announced today, check out our roundup .

items.title: CONFIRMED: Microsoft Hands Halo to Call of Duty Developer Activision as Part of Seismic Xbox Studios Shakeup
items.excerpt: Microsoft has today confirmed that the next mainline Halo game will be developed by Call of Duty maker Activision, with mass layoffs hitting Halo Studios amid a significant restructure of its Xbox studios setup.
items.content_text: Microsoft has today confirmed that the next mainline Halo game will be developed by Call of Duty maker Activision, with mass layoffs hitting Halo Studios amid a significant restructure of its Xbox studios setup. Xbox announced 268 layoffs today "across Halo Studios, other first-party studios, and the XGS management and central functions layer" as part of the ongoing cuts first announced in July . The layoffs, the majority of which are at Halo Studios, come as part of new Xbox boss Asha Sharma’s “reset” of Microsoft's gaming business that had already seen 1,600 staff lose their jobs in the summer. At the time, Microsoft said another 1,600 staff on top would also go this financial year. "The actions completed since July, inclusive of the studio divestitures, bring us roughly three-quarters of the way through previously announced restructuring," Xbox Chief Content Officer Matt Booty said in a blog post . "I am deeply grateful for what our colleagues have built, and I know how difficult today will be for those leaving and the teams around them." With Halo Studios gutted, Microsoft has handed Halo to Activision. Activision will develop "the next Halo title," Booty said, "led by a new, purpose-built team that is separate from ongoing development and plans for Call of Duty. A small team at Halo Studios will continue supporting the Halo community and games in-market." Booty did not say when the next Halo game will come out, or if Activision plans to reboot the series or rotate it into its schedule of releases for Call of Duty, which hasn’t missed an annual release for 20 years. Halo moving to Activision follows a string of tough releases for the franchise under Xbox's stewardship. Microsoft bought the Halo franchise when it purchased its original developer, Bungie, in 2000. Bungie then split from Microsoft to become independent again in 2007, and went to work on looter shooter Destiny as part of a high-profile, 10-year publishing deal with Activision. Meanwhile, Microsoft set up 343 Industries, so named after 343 Guilty Spark from the Halo games, to take Halo into a new era. 2012's Halo 4 was the first Halo game released by 343. It was followed by 2015's Halo 5: Guardians, which in turn was followed by 2021's much-delayed Halo Infinite. Halo Infinite in particular struggled, and this year's Halo: Campaign Evolved, a remake of the beloved first Halo game, suffered problems of its own. In 2024, 343 Industries changed its name to Halo Studios and announced plans to work on multiple new Halo games that would all be developed on Epic's Unreal Engine. The announcements were unveiled in a seven-minute video shown ahead of the Halo World Championship's grand finals, which showcased the results of Project Foundry — an experimental project designed to show a Halo game built using Unreal Engine. While it was not much more than a tech demo, the video offered a glimpse at a fresh beginning for Xbox's flagship franchise in the wake of Halo Infinite's troubled launch. The question is, will any of that work be carried forward by Activision? Meanwhile, Xbox has moved Age of Empires developer World's Edge and Sea of Thieves developer Rare under the Activision umbrella, without confirming the legendary British studio's next game. Rob Kostich, president of Activision issued the following statement: "We’re thrilled to welcome Halo, Rare, and World’s Edge to Activision. It’s an honor and a responsibility that we do not take lightly. These teams and their games have inspired fans around the world for decades. "For Halo, our goal is clear: make the greatest Halo game ever, worthy of its universe and legacy, while staying true to what made players love it in the first place. It is a bold ambition, one that this franchise deserves. We have already begun assembling a purpose-built team, unique in capability and talent, ready and excited to deliver this next chapter with the community. "To the World’s Edge and Rare teams, we can’t wait to get to work together." Outside Activision, Obsidian, developer of Grounded, The Outer Worlds, and Avowed, is now a Bethesda studio, as it begins work on a new Fallout game . Forza Motorsport developer Turn 10 is being merged with Forza Horizon and Fable developer Playground, and Candy Crush developer King now includes Microsoft Casual Games, which operates the likes of Solitaire, Mahjong, and Minesweeper. Microsoft has also signalled its intention to close Hellblade developer Ninja Theory after two separate deals for a sale fell through . As per UK employment law, a consultation with staff has begun. Ninja Theory was working on the third entry in the Hellblade series, called Senua, but that game's future is in doubt . There is no further news on the fate of Blade developer Arkane. Microsoft is currently negotiating with management over the future of the studio , following French employment law, so the process is further behind that of other Xbox studios. Booty said "consultation with Arkane remains underway and is expected to continue through the end of the year." Psychonauts developer Double Fine and South of Midnight studio Compulsion had already managed to navigate their way to independence as part of the Xbox reset. Today, Booty confirmed that Undead Labs has now "successfully transitioned" on "similar terms" and, with a new publisher, will release State of Decay 3 day one on Game Pass. "The goal is to strengthen our franchises and games by operating fewer business units, aligning groups that already work closely together, and focusing our publishing expertise," Booty added. Today’s dramatic news sparks a number of unanswered questions: what does the future of Halo look like? What does Activision plan to do with Rare and Sea of Thieves? And where will the rest of the layoffs Microsoft announced were in the works in July come from? The Xbox reset is the most significant restructure in the history of Microsoft's gaming business, and forms part of Sharma's drive to reach a billion people each day through video games by 2030. It follows continued poor financial results for Xbox and a collapsing profit margin, which Sharma has set about turning around by cutting costs and doubling down on big franchises such as Halo, Minecraft, and Fallout. "Today, our focus should be on supporting those affected and treating one another with care and respect," Booty added. "I will spend time with our studios over the next week. At our October 6 town hall, we will come together as an ALL-XBOX team to reflect on our progress and look ahead to one of the strongest game lineups in our history."
items.title_en: CONFIRMED: Microsoft Hands Halo to Call of Duty Developer Activision as Part of Seismic Xbox Studios Shakeup

items.title: Handing Halo to Activision Makes Business Sense, but Is That Enough To Save the Series?
items.excerpt: The next Halo game will be developed by Activision, but is the slick Call of Duty development pipeline enough to save Master Chief?
items.content_text: This is an IGN opinion piece from Ryan McCaffrey, who worked at Official Xbox Magazine from 2002-2012 during the original Xbox and Xbox 360 era before joining IGN, where he remains “the Xbox guy” and has reviewed several Halo games, including the Master Chief Collection and Halo Infinite . I’ll give Asha Sharma this: she is not afraid to shake things up. Whether you love or hate how she’s run the Xbox business in her first six months as CEO so far, there are no sacred cows with her. Whether it’s slashing Xbox Game Pass prices, nuking an unpopular marketing campaign, restoring console exclusives, telling Obsidian to make a damn Fallout game already , or signing Hideo Kojima after PlayStation cancelled Physint, she is more than willing to flip over some tables to try and get Xbox to a better place. Unfortunately, these decisions have also come paired with a lot of layoffs . To say the situation for all at Xbox is changing would be to put it very lightly. When it comes to the very fundamentals of Xbox’s game DNA, though, Sharma’s latest power move is arguably her most earthshaking one yet. The next mainline Halo will be developed by Activision. Meanwhile, Halo Studios – the series’ custodians since 2011 – has been hit with significant layoffs. Read that again. Halo Studios, once known as 343 Industries – the developer founded purely to create Halo games – will no longer be the creative drivers behind Halo. The keys to the Warthog have been taken away and given to Activision, makers of Call of Duty and the crown jewel of Microsoft’s $69 billion acquisition . The company had to crawl through regulatory broken glass in order to get approval for such a move, so I suppose this is one way to help further justify that kind of expense. This doesn’t reflect well on Xbox’s handling of Halo over the past 15 years. You know you f*cked up pretty bad when the developer that was renamed to Halo Studios less than a year ago is now no longer making the next big Halo game. Like, holy shit. Let that sink in for a minute. But from where I sit, Halo Studios’ issues have never been with raw talent. I absolutely loved Halo 4’s campaign that centered on Master Chief and Cortana’s relationship, but its multiplayer failed to live up to the Halo standard. The opposite happened with Halo 5, whose awful campaign sat alongside a phenomenally good multiplayer. And Halo Infinite finally put two great halves together …for a minute, until the modern needs of maintaining a living multiplayer shooter couldn’t be met by the studio. Instead, the problem has always seemingly been with management. From a reported reliance on an ever-cycling crop of contractors, to having to onboard every one of those said contractors with Halo’s proprietary Blam/Slipspace engine, it made the studio wildly inefficient. I’ve also personally heard from a well-placed source in the past week that leadership is “ineffective” and “makes me facepalm on a regular basis.” You know you f*cked up pretty bad when the developer that was renamed to Halo Studios less than a year ago is now no longer making the next big Halo game. But one source does not a complete narrative make. Let’s instead look at the results. We are already less than three months away from Halo Infinite’s fifth anniversary. And, based on the “reboot” of 343 Industries under the new Halo Studios name, its change of leadership, and shift from the proprietary Slipspace engine to Unreal Engine 5, the chances that the existing development structure could ship a new big Halo game in the next five years seems slim at best. Sharma, who has already made it clear she wants Xbox to take a franchise-first approach to what it invests its resources into, must’ve come to the same conclusion. Giving the series to Activision says one thing above all else to me: she wants a Halo game soon. And Activision, whether you love it or hate it, does have a pretty sterling track record of getting big-budget blockbuster games done in a timely fashion. They’re not always great games (see last year’s Black Ops 7), but they’re usually at least pretty good, and they always ship on time. Has a Call of Duty ever missed a holiday ship date? Not that I can recall – that’s the power of multiple support studios working together. So from that purely business perspective, handing Halo to Activision makes perfect sense. But what about creatively? That’s a more difficult question to answer. Activision undoubtedly has a ton of talent in-house, but Infinity Ward doesn’t seem like it’ll be escaping the Call of Duty salt mines anytime soon after successfully rebooting itself over its last few projects. Sledgehammer, meanwhile, has seemingly fallen out of favor following its tenure on some of Call of Duty’s weakest projects in recent years – Vanguard and Modern Warfare 3. That leaves two likely candidates in my eyes: Treyarch and Raven. Treyarch has arguably been Activision’s most dependable cash factory since it first created the Black Ops sub-franchise back in 2010. It was a success story born out of disaster, following Infinity Ward’s implosion and much of the studio’s founding team departing to form Respawn. Black Ops went on to become the flagship brand for many Call of Duty fans, particularly following the titan that was BLOPS 2. That winning streak came to a screeching halt last year, though, when Black Ops 7 released to middling reviews and disappointing sales . Perhaps that’s the signal that Treyarch needs a new focus. Interestingly, the studio recently said that it was “ ready to make something new ,” a quote which looks awfully suspicious given Sharma’s latest big move. Putting Treyarch in charge of Halo would, in my opinion, be the safest move. Halo needs help, and Treyarch has been Activision’s most reliable studio that has a proven track record of elevating the world’s biggest franchise. A lot of Halo fans understandably hate the idea of the series starting afresh, but honestly, I think it’s time. There’s another possibility, though: Raven Software. The pride of the Wisconsin game development scene has been stuck on Call of Duty for what feels like an eternity, but before that, its resume consisted of some absolute bangers. Heretic, Hexen, Quake 4, Star Trek Voyager: Elite Force, Star Wars Jedi Knight 2, Soldier of Fortune, and the 2009 Wolfenstein reboot are all examples of its FPS pedigree. Putting Raven in charge of Halo would be the bolder pick, if you ask me, and I’d be fired up if the studio got the call. No matter who’s developing the next mainline Halo game, however, this move only makes me even more confident in a prediction I’ve been making for a while now on Podcast Unlocked: that the next major Halo game isn’t going to be Halo 7, or a sequel to Halo Infinite. It feels like far too much time has passed for a direct successor to make sense. Instead, I think what’s next is going to be a reboot. A lot of Halo fans understandably hate the idea of the series starting afresh, but honestly, I think it’s time – especially now that the franchise is changing hands. By the time Activision is ready to roll, we’ll be 30 years deep, give or take, into the Halo canon. There are entire generations of players who missed out on some of Master Chief’s most important chapters. And considering Campaign Evolved was surely Halo’s first and last appearance on a PlayStation console, now that Sharma has made exclusives a priority again, a re-run of those formative years for a wider audience of players is no longer necessary. The reality is that it will be a new team picking up the mantle following a multi-year pause in Halo’s story, and that team is going to have its own ideas. Campaign Evolved isn’t just a dead end when it comes to re-establishing the canon – it’s potentially also a technological loose end. Think about it: if one of the Call of Duty studios takes over, and Sharma wants Halo back on shelves as quickly as possible, you’d only slow that team down by having them pivot to Campaign Evolved’s Unreal Engine 5 when they’ve spent the past 15+ years working with Call of Duty’s proprietary tools. Those teams’ entire development pipelines are built around the bespoke IW engine and its unified toolset. And, for all the creative faults you could pick with Call of Duty, it’s hard to criticize them from a technical perspective. There’s almost zero chance that process gets messed with. Take all of that together and I just don’t see Activision picking up where Halo Studios left off in any way, be it narratively or otherwise. So, can Activision save Halo? The cynical answer would be, “Well, they can’t do any worse.” But the real answer is: maybe. It depends on which studio and which team is entrusted with this billion-dollar task. Halo was the biggest first-person shooter series in the world before being dethroned by Call of Duty. How crazy is it that the very same people who defeated it are now being asked to resurrect it? If I’m being honest, though, as talented as Treyarch and Raven are, neither would be my first in-house pick at Xbox to revive Halo. I’d pick id Software (who might be done with Doom for now ) or MachineGames (who is reportedly busy with the conclusion to its Wolfenstein series). But both Treyarch and Raven are fully capable. Here’s hoping that whoever’s name is on the next Halo understands the assignment and is afforded every resource available to get it done properly.
items.title_en: Handing Halo to Activision Makes Business Sense, but Is That Enough To Save the Series?

items.title: Heart of the Beast Review: Brad Pitt and His Combat Dog Go Ruffin' It in the Wild
items.excerpt: Heart of the Beast is a gripping wilderness survival film that will work especially well on dog lovers and those who like to see Brad Pitt get beaten up.
items.content_text: The lead actor in the new survival drama Heart of the Beast possesses rugged, movie star good looks, does almost all his own stunts, and delivers an understated, deeply moving performance. Brad Pitt is also in this movie. Pitt’s great here, too, but the titular heart of this gripping and emotional film is the dog, who is a very, very good boy indeed. The movie even opens on the soulful face of Odin (real name Uber) , a former US Army combat dog who bears scars, has titanium in his mouth, and a prosthetic leg from injuries suffered in war. His handler/owner is James Belmont (Pitt), a now-retired Green Beret whose face we don’t clearly see until a few moments into the film. As much as James is the protagonist, the film is largely seen through the eyes of Odin. James and Odin also both suffer from PTSD due to their combat experiences (yes, dogs get PTSD, too ). But they have each other, and the bond between them is stronger than steel, a mutual devotion and dependence that keeps them going after James’ plane crashes during a camping trip in the remote wilds of Alaska. After suffering a heart attack while piloting his Cessna, James is put through the wringer as he and Odin (aka Odie) battle the elements, the terrain, and the wildlife over the next several days as they hike roughly 50 miles to reach the nearest road and get help. Assuredly directed by David Ayer from a heartfelt screenplay by Cameron Alexander, Heart of the Beast throws nearly every survival scenario possible at James and Odin. From the unrelenting challenges of navigating the land to enduring gnarly injuries to storms to wolves and a grizzly bear, James and Odin encounter everything that could kill you in the woods except for a masked, machete-wielding serial killer. I was emotionally invested in every moment of their brutal journey because of their relationship. There are as many “please don’t make me cry” moments in Heart of the Beast as there are “God, that looks excruciating” ones, with both James and Odin coming to each other’s aid to help them survive (although, in truth, the dog is pretty useless when it comes to setting up and breaking down campsites!). Heart of the Beast isn’t as overtly emotionally manipulative as you might expect from a dog movie, simply letting Odin’s face and reactions do the work. But Brad Pitt also makes their whole dynamic work so well because of his deeply human performance. As tough and quiet as James is, his wounded soul and world-weariness are made clear just by Pitt’s eyes. That‘s some damn fine eye acting there, Brad Pitt, especially in the film’s closing moments. And in a career that’s seen him get famously battered and bloodied in films like Fight Club, Snatch, Mr. and Mrs. Smith, Bullet Train, Fury, and even Meet Joe Black , to name a few, Brad Pitt gets the absolute shit kicked out of him for about three-quarters of Heart of the Beast’s run time. I can’t imagine just how physically grueling this shoot must have been for him. Less effective are all the flashbacks to James and Odin’s combat experiences, not because they are poorly done but because they don’t convey much new information to the viewer. How both James and Odin ended up with their physical and psychological torments was made perfectly clear during a brief scene with a retired miner (J.K. Simmons) whom they encounter before the plane crash. The flashbacks could’ve been pared down, as they do tend to occasionally interrupt the flow. It’s a testament to how much I cared about James and Odin that I wanted the film to cut back to them and not leave me hanging. Finally, on a technical level, I need to shout out the sumptuous landscape porn cinematography by Mauro Fiore and the haunting score by Jared Michael Fry. However, the CGI wolves and grizzly bear stick out like sore thumbs (although they’re nowhere near as bad as the CG dog in Call of the Wild ). I understand the practical reasons why they had to be used, but the attention they draw distracts from the otherwise very realistic look of the film.
items.title_en: Heart of the Beast Review: Brad Pitt and His Combat Dog Go Ruffin' It in the Wild

items.title: DCU Chief James Gunn Hits Back at Lanterns Criticism Over 'Killing' Hal Jordan 'Right Away'
items.excerpt: DC Universe co-CEO James Gunn has hit back at criticism of HBO show Lanterns for apparently killing Hal Jordan “right away.”
items.content_text: DC Universe co-CEO James Gunn has hit back at criticism of HBO show Lanterns for apparently killing Hal Jordan “right away.” The first episode of Lanterns showed a murdered Hal Jordan, played by Kyle Chandler, in 2026 before going back in time to 2016 to tell a seemingly unrelated story. Warning! Spoilers for Lanterns follow… Showing the much-loved Hal Jordan with a hole in his head in the first episode of the show sparked a significant backlash from fans who had waited years for his live-action depiction in the DCU. Episode 6 doubled down on this by showing Hal’s funeral. But there are question marks hanging over Hal’s death. Indeed, some aren’t convinced he’s dead at all. Following the conclusion of Episode 5, Lanterns has moved back to 2026 and switched into “whodunnit?” mode, with the central storyline revolving around John Stewart’s bid to solve the mystery of Hal’s murder. Some fans believe that over the course of the final two episodes, it will be revealed that the real Hal Jordan is alive and kicking, and the frozen corpse we saw in Episode 1 was a copy of some kind. (We recently explored the many ways Lanterns could explain that Hal is still alive .) Still, some fans are very upset at Hal’s apparent death, and are sending angry messages to James Gunn on social media about it. Gunn actually responded to one person who had this to say: “Maybe you should try and at least respect the characters that made the comics popular. Killing Hal off right away after we have waited 15 years to see him on screen again was the worst thing you could have done.” Gunn clearly didn’t like that, and in his response dropped a clue that fans who think Hal is alive are on the right track. “Hal's the star of TV series & he's in all the episodes so far,” Gunn began. “It's more live action screen time than all the live action screen time he's had combined throughout history. Kyle is amazing in the role. We more than respect him. We love him, despite his imperfections. Us knowing the time of his death, if that's exactly what that is, is absolutely not the same thing as killing him off right away. Hal is a big reason why the show is so popular with fans & non fans alike; sorry if you don't like it.” Gunn’s position on this is clear: he feels like Hal’s had plenty of time on-screen over the course of the show, and it’s true he’s played a starring role in all the episodes so far. But it’s the line about his death that is being highlighted by fans: “Us knowing the time of his death, if that's exactly what that is, is absolutely not the same thing as killing him off right away.” “... if that’s exactly what that is,” is a line that, for some fans, pretty much confirms that there’s more to Hal’s death than it seems. Certainly, Chandler’s portrayal of Hal Jordan has gone down well with fans, who would love to see the character continue in the ongoing DCU. While there’s no suggestion he’s in next year’s Superman sequel, Man of Tomorrow, perhaps Gunn could see Chandler reprise the role in some other project, or maybe even a Lanterns Season 2. Nathan Fillion’s Guy Gardner, however, is proving to be a throughline for the DCU. He’s in Superman, Peacemaker Season 2, Lanterns, and is expected in Man of Tomorrow.
items.title_en: DCU Chief James Gunn Hits Back at Lanterns Criticism Over 'Killing' Hal Jordan 'Right Away'

items.title: Lanterns: Could Hal Jordan Still Be Alive?
items.excerpt: Don't count Hal Jordan out yet on Lanterns. Here's why the iconic Green Lantern might not be as dead as he seems...
items.content_text: Spoilers follow for Lanterns Episodes 1 through 6. When Lanterns, the latest DC Universe show, debuted on HBO last month, it immediately hit many fans where it hurts with the revelation that Hal Jordan – the Green Lantern that so many of us grew up with – was being killed off . It was the first episode of his show, and there he was with a hole in his head, half frozen. What the heck! Which isn’t to say that Kyle Chandler’s take on the character was a one and done. No, thanks to Lanterns being set across multiple time periods, we’ve been able to zero in on his relationship with his successor, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), in the 2016 era, plus we’ve seen some of the character’s earlier exploits as well, albeit briefly. But, of course, the 2026 time period features a dead Hal, including his funeral in Episode 6, “Bad Optics.” But here’s the thing: Are we really sure Hal Jordan is dead? This is a superhero show, after all, albeit one gussied up like a rural crime thriller. We’ve still got two episodes left, and there are some clues that Hal maybe, just maybe, isn’t gone yet. Let’s take a look… The Show Has Already Had a Bunch of Aliens Posing as Humans Think about it: Everyone from Poorna Jagannathan’s Zoe Macon to Paul Ben-Victor’s Antaan to freaking Laura Linney’s character are aliens (or alien constructs) disguised as humans. And they’re just the examples who are played by noteworthy actors! Usually we’ve only seen these extraterrestrials in their human forms, with the exception of Linney’s Lianna – who’s one of the Guardians of the Universe who created the Manhunters and the Green Lantern Corps, by the way – when she briefly shape-shifted into her true form earlier in the season. The point is, Lanterns is full of characters walking around looking like and pretending to be something they are not. Is it so far-fetched to think that Hal’s dead body isn’t the real Hal? The last time we saw him alive was right after John punched him out in the diner, and Hal was clearly scared of something at that point, a state of mind we’ve never really seen him in on this show before. This wors- for-wear version of Hal pleaded with John to not reveal to anyone that his former mentee had been there, so there was obviously something going on that had Hal worried. Did he know he was about to face certain death, and he didn’t want John to be implicated in it? Or perhaps Hal knew there was some kind of bigger plan afoot that would involve the faking of his death, and he still didn’t want John to be connected to it? Is it so far-fetched to think that Hal’s dead body isn’t the real Hal? The bottom line is someone like Hal, with his decades of experience and otherworldly connections, could surely figure out a way to fake his own death with a duplicate alien body if he wanted to. And speaking of friends in high places… Hal’s Old Buddy Sinestro Just Broke Out of Space Jail In this week’s episode, it’s confirmed the Green Lantern of 2026 is definitely not John Stewart, but rather Guy Gardner (Nathan Fillion), who visits John while he’s stuck in a jail cell in Rushville, Nebraska. During their not-at-all contentious chat, Guy reveals that Hal’s old mentor, and former Green Lantern himself, Sinestro (Ulrich Thomsen) has been broken out of “Spazkaban” – aka Space Azkaban (!)... basically the Guardians’ version of prison for the worst of the worst. And not just that, but Guy says that the first suspect for who might’ve helped Sinestro escape would’ve been Hal Jordan, if Hal didn’t have an alibi – namely being in jail himself on Earth. The only problem with that logic is it assumes that was the actual Hal who was in jail! We first met Sinestro, albeit briefly, at the end of Episode 2 when Hal flew to space to talk with his old frenemy and try to pump him for information about the Manhunters. It was during that discussion – as we would later learn in Episode 4 – that Sinestro gave Hal some interesting advice, as he pointed out that John’s fearlessness would also mean he’d be “arrogant, overly confident, [and] thus blindly oblivious to your true intent.” It’s almost like Sinestro was giving Hal a roadmap as to how he could pull the wool over John’s eyes. The obvious read here is that Hal took this advice and that’s what led to the disaster in Rushville in Episode 5 , but could it be that he was playing a much longer game? After all, the writers wouldn’t just tell that Sinestro broke out of jail, only to then just drop that story thread, right? So whatever’s going on with that character, it would seem odd for it to not involve Hal… There’s Something Fishy About Sheriff Kane’s Son Noah Macon… So many secrets in this town! First there was the reveal that Kelly Macdonald’s Sheriff Kerry Kane had some kind of a dark past in Gotham City , and became – along with much of the town’s population – a member of Zoe Macon’s covert protection force as a means to escape that history. Zoe herself had the whole “I’m actually a Manhunter” thing going, and then there are all those aliens disguised as humans who we already talked about. But now, in the 2026 timeline, we also have to wonder what the truth is regarding Noah Macon (Shea Pritchard). A high school football star that the whole town seems to be interested in, it’s obvious that the teen is a gifted athlete. He also seems to be a… great person, writing to FEMA over and over again until they repaired his school. (“He’s a natural-born leader,” his mom says.) And while Zoe wasn’t a biological relative as far as we know, she was his grandmother by marriage. The timing is certainly right for Zoe to have somehow created him when Kerry moved to Rushville. Is Noah also a Manhunter, if that’s the case? If this theory does pan out, I’m still not sure how it would connect to Hal faking his death… unless Hal has joined Kerry as a member of the Manhunter protection force (MPF?), and somehow this is all a ruse to draw out whatever Manhunter threat might still be out there. It’s Halogram Time You know, there’s one other possibility here, which is that, yes, Hal Jordan is in fact dead. But if we ever do get more Lanterns – we know a Season 2 is in the works, even if it hasn’t been officially greenlit yet – it could be that Kyle Chandler’s holographic version of Hal – his “Halogram” – would just be a way to keep the actor around, even if the actual Hal is dead and buried (in his suit but without his ring, of course). The Halogram is one of the funnest aspects of the show, and he also represents a kinder, gentler version of Hal, which would give Chandler a different aspect of the character to play in a new season. Plus, he gets all the good lines… To quote the Halogram, “Goddamit!” Talk to Scott Collura @scottcollura.bsky.social , or listen to his Star Trek podcast, Transporter Room 3 . Or do both!
items.title_en: Lanterns: Could Hal Jordan Still Be Alive?

items.title: 'Risky and Gutsy': Resident Evil Movie Star Austin Abrams Reveals His First Reaction to The Film's 'Shocking' Finale
items.excerpt: Resident Evil movie star Austin Abrams has recalled his initial reaction to the film's finale, which he believes is "crazy and shocking."
items.content_text: Resident Evil movie star Austin Abrams has recalled his initial reaction to the film's finale, which he believes is "crazy and shocking." Warning: spoilers for Resident Evil follow... Zach Cregger's enjoyable Resident Evil film follows Abrams' everyman courier Bryan as he transports a bag of medical supplies into a deadly zombie apocalypse. Unfortunately, as you'll know from watching the film, Bryan ends up not making it out of Raccoon City alive. It's a particularly sad ending for Bryan as he's never able to reconnect with his pregnant girlfriend, or make amends with her after an earlier argument. Despite fighting off waves of undead and recording a message of reconciliation for her, Bryan succumbs to his injuries and turns into a monster, just as a cure is produced. Cregger's ending is certainly a bold choice, and one that differs from the heroic end featured in every Resident Evil game. But Abrams himself is clearly a fan of this story's finale, and described the ending as a "risky and gutsy" decision by Cregger, in an era where downbeat endings are now rarer to avoid bumming out audiences and killing a movie's chance for word-of-mouth recommendations. "I've been living with it for a while now, but I thought it was crazy and shocking when I first read it," Abrams told The Hollywood Reporter . "I love that Zach takes those risks. You follow this one guy the whole time, so hopefully you’re enjoying watching him and rooting for him. Then to have him not make it is really risky and gutsy, which is what I love about all of Zach’s work. So I was surprised by it, but I also loved that he would take that chance. "With a lot of movies nowadays, they’re a little too afraid to do something like that — to kill off a character you really like," he concluded. "And if they do, the blow is softened in some way so it doesn't hurt too much. Whereas a lot of older films don’t do that; they just rip your heart out. We're here to feel, man. We're here to go through something. So I'm just appreciative that Zach is willing to take a risk like that." With all of that said, however, we learned this week that Cregger still tweaked the film's ending in post production using material he'd already shot — if anything to make things even more tragic. There's details here of how things would have originally planned out .

items.title: 'I'm Too Old': Marvel Star Says He's Officially Retired From His Beloved Guardians of the Galaxy Role as Rocket Raccoon
items.excerpt: Marvel actor Sean Gunn has officially retired from his role playing Guardians of the Galaxy and Avengers hero Rocket Raccoon.
items.content_text: Marvel actor Sean Gunn has officially retired from his role playing Guardians of the Galaxy and Avengers hero Rocket Raccoon. After five films and one holiday TV special, Gunn has said he's now "too old" to provide the performance capture for the beloved Rocket (whose voice is then dubbed in post-production by Bradley Cooper). Speaking to podcast host Brandon Davis , the Gilmore Girls legend said he had made the decision to depart his role as Rocket after recently turning 50, and noticing that the amount of crouching he'd had to perform for the part was beginning to have an effect on his "physiology." On set, behind the scenes footage has featured Gunn scuttling around the legs of his Marvel co-stars while squatting down in what he describes as a "catcher's crouch" position. Thankfully, Gunn could also stretch his legs and stand up to also play Kraglin, the Ravager who ultimately ends the sci-fi saga as a fully paid-up Guardians member. "Everyone thinks it's my knees but it's really my feet and my ankles," Gunn said, describing the physical difficulty he has faced after portraying Rocket Raccoon. "Because I'm in a catcher's crouch and I'm pivoting a lot on my points of contact with the ground... I'm doing a lot of pivoting in my ankles and feet. And over the years I think it had a little bit of an effect on my physiology. "My knees are fine but since I turned 50 a couple of years ago I am retired from Rocket," he admitted. "Not that they've called but if they did, I don't think I could do the motion reference for Rocket anymore. I'm too old." When might we see Rocket again? It's hard to say. Marvel is yet to confirm its future plans for the Guardians of the Galaxy, which remains a hugely popular team of characters, though one whose story has reached a natural conclusion. Gamora is off with the Ravagers, Drax and Nebula are looking after an array of children, while Mantis has also gone off to find her own path. Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 ends with a new team forming, featuring Rocket, Groot, and Kraglin joined by Adam Warlock, Cosmo the Space Dog, and Phyla. It's unclear if any of the above characters will ever return to the MCU, and it seems unlikely we'll get another Guardians of the Galaxy movie any time soon, with its writer and director James Gunn (yes, Sean Gunn's brother) now heading up the DCU. But Marvel has promised that Chris Pratt's Star-Lord will appear at some point (our best guess would be in Avengers: Secret Wars). But even if Rocket Raccoon is invited back for the Multiverse Saga's big finale, it'll be someone else who squatted down to portray him instead. Image credit: Eric McCandless/Disney via Getty Images.

items.title: The Legend of Zelda Movie Actress Posts Cryptic Tease, Raising Hopes for an Imminent Trailer
items.excerpt: The Legend of Zelda movie star Bo Bragason has raised hopes of an imminent trailer release for Nintendo's upcoming film.
items.content_text: The Legend of Zelda movie star Bo Bragason has raised hopes of an imminent trailer release for Nintendo's upcoming film. With just seven months to go until The Legend of Zelda arrives in theatres, Nintendo and Sony (which is distributing the film) are yet to show anything of it in motion. Sure, we've had a few photos of Bragason in costume as Zelda , alongside House of the Dragon actor Benjamin Evan Ainsworth as Link. But there has been no sign of a teaser, and still no official confirmation of the film's wider cast — despite many unofficial reports now having emerged. Could all of that change today? Fans certainly believe so, as Bragason posted on Instagram last night to say she was "excited 4 tomorrow." Bragason regularly posts on Instagram about her upcoming projects, though has acknowledged she can say nothing specific at all about The Legend of Zelda, which Nintendo is keeping under lock and key. Fans had hoped we'd see something more of the film in this month's recent Zelda-focused Nintendo Direct , but in reality there was little to add. Nintendo confirmed that The Legend of Zelda would be the movie's name, and acknowledged it would be an original story inspired by the franchise so far, rather than a direct adaptation of any particular game. Originally announced in 2023, The Legend of Zelda is helmed by Maze Runner and Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes director Wes Ball, while Nintendo's legendary Shigeru Miyamoto is listed as a co-producer, alongside Marvel production veteran Avi Arad. The movie was shot last winter in New Zealand, with the Middle-earth-like location now doubling for Hyrule. Unofficially, it's been reported that Dichen Lachman (Severance) will play Impa, while Uli Latukefu (Black Adam) will play Ganondorf. These will be joined by other castmates such as Yvonne Strahovski, Lydia Peckham and the late Sam Neill . While their roles have yet to be disclosed , Deadline reported that the former will be playing a "queen" character. Could we see them confirmed officially today? Time will tell. But what we do know for sure is that The Legend of Zelda is currently set to arrive in theaters on April 30, 2027. Image credit: Jason Mendez/Getty Images for Prime Video.

items.content_text: IGN can today reveal three new Pokémon card designs from the upcoming set Pokémon TCG: Mega Evolution — Delta Reign. Due to launch on November 6, this latest batch of Mega Evolution-themed cards includes creatures such as Mega Malamar, Mega Golurk and Mega Rayquaza, with over 135 designs in total. Today, we can show off our first look at starter Sprigatito, the Grass Cat Pokémon, as well as both of its evolutions, Floragato and Meowscarada. Sprigatito's design shows the cute kitty settling down for a late morning nap on a trainer's bed. Its 70 HP is decent, though its Play Rough attack lacks a little punch. It's lucky, then, that you can evolve Sprigatito into Floragato, with 90 HP and the Slash attack for a chunkier 60 damage. With that on the board, you're on your way to playing Meowscarada ex, which lands with a solid 320 HP and the strong Magical Bullet attack, that can deal a whopping 120 damage to its opponent, and another 120 damage to any damaged benched Pokémon. As with all ex cards, though, Meowscarada will count for two prizes if knocked out. Pokémon TCG: Mega Evolution — Delta Reign will be the next set to launch following the current Pokémon 30th Anniversary release, which arrived last week to huge demand , queues , fights , and ultimately some disappointment from scalpers who haven't been able to turn their usual profits . items.title: How Long Is Silent Hill: Townfall?
items.excerpt: Five different IGN editors played through Silent: Hill Townfall in five different ways to find out how long Konami's new survival horror is, depending on playstyle.
items.content_text: Konami's latest game in the nu-Silent Hill era has arrived, and as is the case with previous entries in the series, Townfall boasts a handful of endings to unlock and an even bigger handful of scares. But how long does it all take? We got five different members of the IGN team, who all played Silent Hill: Townfall very differently, to share their time. So whether you’re a completionist, or just someone who’s only interested in the story, you’ll learn just how long you’ll be spending in St. Amelia depending on your playstyle. How Long is Silent Hill: Townfall? Our fastest player finished Silent Hill: Townfall in 12 hours and 37 minutes. Our “slowest” player spent 15 hours and 15 minutes before credits rolled. Everyone plays games differently, so read on for more details about how everyone played, how long it took to reach the credits, and some of the individual statistics from their end-of-game report card. Once you've finished the game yourself, be sure to submit your times on How Long To Beat and see how your time compares! Playstyle: Trying to Find Everything Player: Jesse Gomez Completion Time: 12 hours and 55 minutes With just under 34 hours of playtime under my belt, a few restless dreams between two separate playthroughs, and three wildly different endings, my intended aim was clear: to experience as much of Silent Hill: Townfall as possible. To start, I chose the Normal/Hinted difficulty, which Townfall recommends when you select new game in the main menu. That combo set me up for a 12 hour, 55 minute clear time, reaching the "Forever" ending. As far as I could tell at the time, this was a largely "positive" outcome, but I knew there had to be more to unravel with a "true" ending, so to speak. Once I hit New Game Plus, however, it became pretty clear that new collectables had snuck into this seaside town. I quickly abandoned Simon's hunt for the truth to instead get the bizarre secret endings, something that’s a Silent Hill tradition and well worth seeing for yourself. You can get both of these in the same playthrough with some additional puzzle-solving, combing over every inch of Townfall, and some tactical saving. Despite experiencing true horror in the form of the auxiliary line B puzzle for nearly an hour, and pushing myself through a New Game Plus puzzle that had me on the verge of tears, I'm sure I could've cleared Townfall a lot sooner. But what's a Silent Hill game if not incredibly obtuse and wholly rewarding all at the same time? Playstyle: Stealthy and Cautious Player: Matt Purslow Completion Time: 15 hours and 15 minutes The fog-shrouded island of St. Amelia is the stage for a different kind of Silent Hill compared to what we’ve had over the past couple of years. Where the Silent Hill 2 remake was a traditional survival horror and Silent Hill f went heavy on the combat, Townfall features comparatively fewer enemies and far fewer options for eliminating them. As a result, combat is downplayed and each individual foe feels more like a mini “stalker” enemy than a regular mob. This design influenced my entire playstyle: for me, Townfall was a stealth game. My slower, more cautious approach means I clocked up a slightly longer time compared to most of my colleagues – it took me 15 hours and 15 minutes to complete my first run of the story. Rather than bludgeoning every enemy with my pipe, I’d use bricks and bottles to distract them and create openings for myself. My final stats claim I spent four minutes and 15 seconds hiding, but that only accounts for when I was concealed in lockers – I spent many, many more minutes hiding behind cover or locked in sheds and bathrooms as I tracked enemies on the CRTV and planned my next move. I chose my victims carefully, only killing foes that blocked pathways I’d frequently use as I looped back and forth around each location. My total kill count was 76, most of them racked up when the pressure really kicks in during the story’s final chapters. This approach netted me the “Abandoned” ending, which felt thematically appropriate for the story, but definitely leaves the door open for more discoveries. And so I’m looking forward to diving into New Game Plus to take another crack at solving St. Amelia’s troubles. Playstyle: Story Mode Player: Dale Driver - Story Mode Completion Time: 12 hours and 37 minutes I really enjoy the stories of Silent Hill, particularly their ambiguity and puzzles, but I've been less engaged with their combat recently, so I decided to try Silent Hill: Townfall on Story Mode to make getting through fights a easier. With this set up I clocked a final time of 12 hours and 37 minutes, reaching the "Abandoned" ending. In Story Mode, enemies drop a little easier, and there are more supplies in storage cupboards and drawers, so I found myself taking on more monsters than my colleagues did, clocking up a whopping 105 kills during my time in St. Amelia. One thing Story Mode doesn’t help with, though, is the puzzles, and a few particular late-game ones really added significantly to my playtime. I found a few particularly obtuse (or maybe I was just being really dumb) but I could easily see a second playthrough taking half the time when you know the solutions. And I plan to do just that, knowing there are new weapons to find and four new endings to discover. After all, the story is what I love the most, so I can’t wait to learn more about it. Playstyle: Going For the True Ending Player: Lauren Harper Completion Time: 15 hours and 8 minutes It took me around 15 hours and 8 minutes to finish my first playthrough of Silent Hill: Townfall. As a member of the guides team at IGN, I always find that it takes me a bit longer than everyone else (my current overall play time shows 44 hours). I’m often writing while I play and taking screenshots of everything as I run back and forth, double-checking each drawer, cabinet, and locked room to make sure I don’t miss anything in terms of collectibles. That being said, I did actually miss a few of the 85 possible discoveries. What I didn’t miss out on was the opportunity to use every weapon in the game, and I racked up a kill count of 92. I also finished up with the "Abandoned" ending on my first go. I then played through again and decided to take on as much of a pacifist run as possible. I avoided killing anything unless it was absolutely necessary and opted for a stealthier approach using every method of distraction I could find. Despite a more considered playthrough, because I knew all the puzzle solutions and locker combinations on my second go, my second run came in at 8 hours and 24 minutes, with just five saves, but an enormous number of healing items used. This netted me the "Justice" ending. Is this the "true" ending? You'll have to play to find out. Now, I’m off to complete another New Game Plus run to hunt down anything new and find those remaining collectibles so our guide is complete. Playstyle: Reviewing Player: Tristan Ogilvie Completion Time: 13 hours and 36 minutes Given that I was reviewing Silent Hill: Townfall for IGN , I tried to be as thorough as possible with my search through the small town of St. Amelia and beyond. Playing on the Normal difficulty settings for both combat and puzzles, it took me 13 hours and 36 minutes from the moment Simon washed up on the Scottish shoreline through to the intense final moments of its climactic boss fight. Although admittedly, roughly 30 of those minutes were spent stuck on one of the late game puzzles that had me properly flummoxed. Curse you, auxiliary line B! According to the endgame stats page, I made 78 out of the 85 discoveries and found 9 out of the 13 phone numbers, so clearly there was the odd optional room here and there that I overlooked. Although I spent much of the early hours opting for stealth and avoiding enemy confrontations, I still managed to murder 92 of Townfall’s ghouls by the story’s end, with the vast majority of those occurring in the second half of the game once more powerful weapons were made available. Ultimately, the ending I received was the one dubbed "Abandoned". I definitely plan to do another run-through on New Game Plus, although it won’t be in the near future because trying to keep up with all the other awesome games coming out this month is a form of survival horror in itself.
items.title_en: How Long Is Silent Hill: Townfall?

items.title: Injustice 3 Leak Reportedly Reveals 2 Playable Characters
items.excerpt: Injustice 3 will feature one character fans will expect and one who perhaps comes as a surprise, according to a fresh leak.
items.content_text: Injustice 3 will feature one character fans will expect and one who perhaps comes as a surprise, according to a fresh leak. MP1st unearthed evidence to suggest the unannounced fighting game will feature both Supergirl and Batwoman on its roster of playable characters. Supergirl comes as no surprise, given her starring role in the nine-year-old Injustice 2. But Batwoman’s inclusion — assuming it’s true — would mark the debut for the character in the mainline Injustice games. Batwoman (Kate Kane) dies in the canon Injustice comics, which suggests someone else has taken up the Batwoman mantle for Injustice 3, Kate Kane didn’t actually die, or the game retcons the events of the book. Either way, this is a superhero story we’re talking about — no-one stays dead forever. Or, as MP1st suggests, Injustice 3 may not continue the story told in Injustice and Injustice 2, but act as a reboot that tells an entirely different story. NetherRealm’s other fighting game franchise, Mortal Kombat, has done this multiple times, so it wouldn’t be a huge surprise with Injustice since it’s been nearly a decade since Injustice 2 came out. Publisher Warner Bros. has yet to announce another Injustice game, despite it being an open secret at this point. Given Paramount looks like it’s finally going to get the green light to complete its $110 billion merger with Warner Bros., perhaps that will provide some clarity on the company’s video game plan, which we know also include Hogwarts Legacy 2 and a new Batman game from Arkham developer Rocksteady. My guess is Injustice 3 — or whatever it’s called — is announced at The Game Awards in December, with a release set for in or around April 2027. In May, NetherRealm development chief Ed Boon said another Mortal Kombat game was in development , which again, didn't come as much of a surprise. Confirmation of another Mortal Kombat game came after 2023’s Mortal Kombat 1 sold 8 million copies, just over half Mortal Kombat 11’s total of 15 million copies sold, as of 2022. Perhaps this new Mortal Kombat game will be released after Injustice 3. The first game in the series, Injustice: Gods Among Us , launched in 2013, with its sequel, Injustice 2 , coming out in 2017. NetherRealm released Mortal Kombat 11 in 2019 and for a time it seemed like the studio would alternate between Mortal Kombat and Injustice games, but it went on to release another Mortal Kombat, the soft reboot that is Mortal Kombat 1, in 2023 instead.

items.title: The Love Hypothesis Review
items.excerpt: The Love Hypothesis review: Ali Hazelwood’s New York Times bestseller gets adapted into a charming rom-com.
items.content_text: The Love Hypothesis streams exclusively on Prime Video starting September 23. Sometimes a rom-com isn’t just a rom-com; such is the case with The Love Hypothesis, a Prime Video movie adaptation of author Ali Hazelwood's 2021 New York Times bestseller. In most cases, that’s a cut-and-dry scenario. However, Hazelwood’s book evolved out of the author’s frustration with how the Star Wars sequels turned out; she, among many, was so frustrated with how the characters of Rey and Kylo Ren/Ben Solo were done dirty in Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker that she “fixed” their outcomes through a creative outpouring of fan fiction. One of them was rewritten as The Love Hypothesis and published, turning into an international BookTok sensation and now a movie. Hazelwood’s book evolved out of the author’s frustration with how the Star Wars sequels turned out. Why all the history? Because The Love Hypothesis has been created with a decidedly modern lens, depending on the audience watching it. For everyone who just enjoys an entertaining rom-com or loved the book, The Love Hypothesis is an accessible, charming watch led by the warm chemistry of the entire cast, especially leads Lili Reinhart and Tom Bateman. For anyone who comes to it from Star Wars fandom and has followed the journey of Hazelwood and her story to this moment in time, the movie is a very meta wink filled with easter eggs tailored just for them. The basic story remains the same: Third-year Stanford University PhD student Olive Smith (Reinhart) is overworked and underfunded in the traditionally male-dominated science world. Her lifeline through it all is best friend Anh (Rachel Marsh), a fellow PhD student who has pulled Olive out of her shell, introduced her to other friends like Malcolm (Jaboukie Young-White), and become her ride-or-die found family. When Jeremy (Nicholas Duvernay), Olive’s one-time crush, shows interest in Anh, Anh won’t do anything about it because their girl code is stronger than mutual attraction. Olive lies that she has a new boyfriend to get Anh to pursue Jeremy, but that backfires when Anh wants in-person details about Olive’s “date,” and a panicked Olive kisses the first man she sees for cover — the departmental Kylo Ren, Dr. Adam Carlsen (Bateman). What starts as a horribly awkward moment becomes a mutually agreed upon ruse between Olive and Adam when he shares that his grant money is under threat of not being released. Stanford is worried that Carlsen is a flight risk to another research institution, so he could use a “girlfriend” to make it seem like he’s got roots and won’t be exiting anytime soon. For both audiences, their public relationship-proving moments escalate into more awkward expressions of intimacy, such as suntan lotion applications and recounting their fictional “meet-cute” to his colleagues. Wisely, director Claire Scanlon ( The People We Hate at the Wedding ) allows these scenes to breathe, heightening their comedic potential and allowing the ensemble to bring out the laughs, of which there are many. Marsh and Young-White are particularly good at pitch-perfect reactions or zingers that lean into the silliness of the “fake dating” scenario while also building a little ecosystem of friendship that drives why Olive is doing what she’s doing. Reinhart and Bateman also absolutely sell the thawing between these two socially awkward dorks into a genuine romance. Yes, in reality they’re both too pretty to ever have that descriptor applied to them, but as Olive and Adam, you buy why they’d hold the world at arms’ length and decide not to do so with one another. Comedically, they’re top notch, and the scenes where they get to express genuine honesty and mutual loneliness with one another percolates into a friendship and bubbling attraction that’s the do-or-die element to any great rom-com. The STEM-centric aspects of the story are watered down in Sarah Rothschild’s script, though an homage sequence to Martha Coolidge’s 1985 science comedy, Real Genius, very much works as it adds a sense of color and context to Olive’s world. Less successful is the science villain of the piece, who gets a lot more time to unfurl his machinations in the book. Here, he isn’t given enough story real estate to be as potent an adversary, or to even rise above a one-note character with clichéd intentions. Fortunately, Rothschild’s screenplay replaces that screen time with more consequential scenes for Olive and Anh, the bedrock for why this “fake dating” operation is even happening. Portraying the strength of their bond is far more worthwhile, underpinning the romantic story with a deeper one about friendship and sisterhood. At its heart, The Love Hypothesis is a gentle satire of romance tropes, especially enemies-to-lovers, and a celebration of female friendship. And for the fans who go all the way back to this story’s Star Wars origins, there are a wealth of easter eggs to find and laugh over, from pointed needle drops to very specific Laura Karpman musical character themes, and even red-and-blue color cameos. The production knows who you are, and they’ve clearly got a sense of humor and respect for the OG fandom. At its heart, The Love Hypothesis is a gentle satire of romance tropes, especially enemies-to-lovers, and a celebration of female friendship. Both sound potentially hokey, but this mostly female creative team understands what made the book a hit and knew how to translate it here. They let the tone be earnest yet firmly tongue-in-cheek, and allow their cast to weave their magic — especially Reinhart and Bateman — giving rom-com lovers the exact chemistry that makes the genre work.
items.title_en: The Love Hypothesis Review

items.title: StarCraft: Tabletop Miniatures Game Review
items.content_text: Long before I deployed my first army of little plastic figures on a table for war, I was mowing down the slithering Zerg and doing battle against the Queen of Blades in StarCraft. The term “Space Marines” I will now, and forever, associate with the Terran army from Blizzard’s classic RTS franchise (despite Games Workshop’s version being older and SC starting off as a 40K RTS). When Archon Studio, a board game developer with an impressive history of adapting massive games for the tabletop, announced they were making a tabletop miniature war game set in this universe, I started clearing off my hobby table in anticipation. Similar to other tabletop war games, standard matches of StarCraft take place over the course of five rounds where players or teams struggle to complete objectives. Instead of picking one from a book, at the start of each game, players will bring two possible choices each for both what the game’s type (i.e. the goals both sides are working to complete) and deployment zones, which dictate where armies and objectives will be placed. From there, the choices are drafted, with one person picking the type and the other the deployment. It’s a system that I found not only works really well but adds to the variety of possible matches you experience. I’m also a big fan of the concept of players supplying the choices themselves, as everyone is submitting options that could benefit their side. The result of that ultimately means both sides will have to deal with a scenario that isn’t quite as ideal as they had hoped for. Where to Buy The best place to buy the StarCraft: Tabetlop Miniatures Game is directly from the official store on Blizzard's website . There you can find the miniatures themselves and the rulebook, but not the two player starter set. You can find the starter set on Amazon or other third-party tabletop retailers, usually at a higher price. In addition to their maps and mission cards, each player brings a host of other cards with them that help define the composition of their armies along with upgrades they have purchased. Faction cards, which are picked before the game, establish the number and variety of slots available in your army, such as how many core units (your basic troops), elites, or heroes (Raynor or Kerrigan, for example) you can include, along with some unique benefits or tags for that specific faction. These tags may be required when selecting which Tactical cards to buy, with these representing various buildings from the RTS games or perks that can impart special bonuses, buffs, or increase the number of supply slots available to your forces. Along with the fact that all the troops and their required information—stats, costs, everything you need to know—are included on handy info cards, I love that I don’t necessarily need to carry around a rulebook whenever I want to play. Instead, I can just throw a small deck of cards into my bag, which is incredibly convenient, and far lighter to carry around. And in practice, it’s really quick and easy to just hand the reference card to the other player if they have a question about an ability, as opposed to book-marking pages in a rule book or handing over a sheet with all the information that has to be parsed through. When it comes to each of the three races’ minis, all of them come in a unique color plastic along with impressive semi-transparent accents that really help to make the models look great. Inside the Starter Set, Terrans feature a muted blue and include orange explosion effect pieces and green healing sprays for the medics, for instance, while Zergs are a pinkish-purple and Protoss a bright yellow with blue energy shields and blades. And yes, there is even a Pylon miniature with a large clear blue crystal, so you can build all the additional pylons you want! The models are impressively detailed and just begging for a sick paint job. Even if you just opt for a primer base coat and a wash, the model details along with the accent parts really help all the units pop and look great on the table. The fact that I was never out of actively participating in the game for longer than a few minutes made me so much more invested StarCraft features a host of design decisions that make it a far more alluring prospect for me to play than other tabletop war games , largely thanks to keeping me more engaged and leaving me with far less downtime than 40k, which is where I have spent the most of my wargaming time. StarCraft adopts a system of alternative activations, meaning that I never have to worry about hour-long stretches of downtime as I wait for my friends to take their entire turn before I can act. From deployment, to moving, to shooting and close combat, the fact that I was never out of actively participating in the game for longer than a few minutes made me so much more invested and excited in games of StarCraft. It turns out that not having to try to remember a strategy you came up with an hour back before you can implement it is actually really nice! The alternating turns is only part of what has really helped StarCraft win me over. Instead of deploying all (or most) of your troops at the very start, all units begin in reserve, with the battlefield only able to field a limited amount of troops at a time. This supply limit, dictated by the mission picked at the start, keeps things more manageable (and timely), with each unit on the field taking up various amounts of that given limit, with squads like the Terran Marines supply value reducing as they lose troops. Then at the start of a brand new round, that limit increases, allowing for fresh and stronger troops to deploy, with that limit removed altogether if the game lasts until the final fifth round. Not only do I appreciate this approach since it removes the likelihood of a disastrous first turn ruining your chances at the start of a long game, but I found it lets players adjust their strategies and approach better mid-game, as the deployment order of troops isn’t set until the moment they are taken out of reserve. So if you really need bodies on the board, you can change your strategy from bringing out your heavy units next round to a couple more squads of zerglings to swarm the field. It also feels more faithful to the original PC RTS , as you build up your army as the game progresses. Movement will still have you busting out your handy-dandy tape measure and combat is still a chaotic symphony StarCraft’s twists don’t stop just at deployment or when you take your turn though, despite its combat feeling a bit familiar if you have played a tabletop war game before. Movement will still have you busting out your handy-dandy tape measure and combat is still a chaotic symphony of rolling handfuls of dice for attacks and defense. The twist the Archon Studio has thrown into the fighting pits is the Surge mechanic. Some weapons units come with a designated “Surge type” with an associated tag, such a “Light” or “Armoured”. When using that weapon against an enemy with a matching tag, some of your successful hits for damage will circumvent the opponent’s armor roll, and will deal damage. It almost turns encounters into a rock-paper-scissors game where there is a clear and impactful incentive to attack units with the right type of counter unit, and adds a satisfying and clever layer of strategy to battles. One unfortunate carry over that StarCraft hasn’t managed to avoid, that plagues the hobby as a whole, is that this can still be a rather pricey game to play. The two player Starter Box which includes a Terran and Zerg army hovers around the $200, with individual army starter sets for Zerg, Protoss, or Terran will set you back $120-$130, with the various squad or hero boxes coming in between the $50 and $80 price point. It’s the world we live in, I suppose, but to Archon Studio’s credit, the full rulebook is available for free along with a handy browser app with the various cards you can use, so if you find yourself with some standard bases, some LEGO miniatures and super glue…

items.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker Update to Add Easier Difficulty Setting for Players Who Don't Want Combat
items.excerpt: The first major The Blood of Dawnwalker update will introduce an easier difficulty option for "people who don't want to experience combat" when it launches in October.
items.content_text: The first major The Blood of Dawnwalker update will introduce an easier difficulty option for "people who don't want to experience combat" when it launches in October. Developer Rebel Wolves' game director, Konrad Tomaszkiewicz, teased the changes coming to the team's breakout vampire RPG during a new interview with Eurogamer . Amongst a batch of combat tweaks and other gameplay changes, one of the highlights for the early October The Blood of Dawnwalker update includes reworked difficulty options for players who don't want to spill too much blood during the story. When the update launches, players will see the new easier difficulty option replace the current easiest mode, called Story Mode, and adopt its name. The version of the mode currently in the game will seemingly be bumped up a peg and given a new name. The Blood of Dawnwalker currently has four difficulty modes – Story, Fair, Challenging, and Duelist – with next month's addition set to bring the total to five. "We will introduce an additional difficulty level, but an easier one, because many people are asking for a more easy difficulty," Tomaszkiewicz said. "The Story mode which we have right now will be a different difficulty — we will call it Demanding or something like this — and we will add a new Story mode which will be even easier for people who don't want to experience the combat, they just want to learn the story and go through the game without this gameplay challenge." How exactly The Blood of Dawnwalker will tackle an easier difficulty mode is unclear. The game director's comment suggests it will cater to those who want to skip combat altogether, though how this will be achieved is unclear. There's no release date for the update just yet, but with its launch set for early October, we won't have to wait too long. Rebel Wolves is also looking into improving gameplay performance, especially for PC users, as well as a fluid option for players to escape fights if they bite off more than they can chew. Other items on the docket include targeting and the camera. Tomaszkiewicz referenced desires from players to tweak how targeting works for Coen and how the upcoming patch will address that. "There will be three hits you need to take off this stun," he said. "We will see how people will react to that because, as I said, it can create another bad feel, but we will see. Maybe people will switch between targets fluently and if they want to just stun, it will be fine, and if they want to stun and hit a few times, it will be also fine. We will see." Everything else set to come to The Blood of Dawnwalker in the October patch has yet to be revealed. Although other features, including new game plus , are confirmed to be in the cards, the team is still charging ahead following its successful launch. It was released for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S September 3 and reached more than 1 million copies sold in just two days . For more on The Blood of Dawnwalker, you can read about how Bandai Namco and Rebel Wolves managed to bring their vision to life on a $40 million budget . You can also learn about how some players are using a mod to bypass one of the game's core mechanics .
